title: Site walk-through and dynamic risk assessment
audience: Garden clean-up workers and crew leaders who assess a site before work and reassess it while work is in progress.
learningOutcomes: Walk a garden site and identify slopes, holes, trip hazards, irrigation components, overhead and buried services, fragile surfaces and public access routes.
Set safe work zones and choose methods that use higher-order controls before personal protective equipment.
Define the triggers that require the risk assessment to be reviewed, and apply the stop-work rule.
Produce a site hazard map that the supervisor can check.

instruction.heading: Why a walk-through comes before any tool
instruction.body: Most garden incidents happen because a hazard was not noticed before the work started. A hose hidden under leaves catches a foot, a paver lifts under a barrow, a sprinkler head is cut by a trimmer, or a child runs out from behind a hedge. A walk-through is a structured look at the site before any equipment is moved. Its purpose is to identify hazards, decide the methods, and set the conditions under which the job will stop. It is not a formality, and it should be repeated whenever the conditions change. Use the walk-through to decide what you can do safely, what needs a different method, and what must be referred. If the site has features that are outside your training or authority, stop, record them and inform the supervisor before you start.

instruction.heading: What to look for on a garden site
instruction.body: Walk the whole area slowly and make notes. Look for slopes and uneven ground where a mower or a loaded barrow can tip. Check for holes, pits, steps and changes of level that are hidden by long grass or leaves. Look at surfaces such as pavers, decking, glass, ponds and steps, and note any that are cracked, loose or slippery. Identify irrigation pipes, valves, controllers and sprinkler heads, and mark them so that they are not cut or driven over. Look up for overhead lines, branches that may be dead or hanging, and any structure that may be damaged by equipment. Look at the ground for buried services, such as electrical cables, gas lines, water pipes and drains, and for signs such as markers, meter boxes and inspection covers. Treat any service you cannot identify as live until a qualified person confirms otherwise. Note where the public, neighbours, children and pets can reach the work area, and where vehicles will be parked and turned.

instruction.heading: Choosing methods and setting work zones
instruction.body: Once you have the hazard list, plan the methods. Use the hierarchy of control. Elimination means removing the hazard before work begins, for example by moving a hose or a planter out of the path. Substitution means using a safer method, for example a hand saw in place of a powered tool near a service box. Separation means keeping people away from the hazard, for example by setting up a barrier, a clear route for barrows and a one-way path for material. Engineering controls include equipment guards, a residual current device on the supply and a stable platform for loads. Administrative controls include a sequence of tasks, a spotter for reversing vehicles and a start and finish briefing. Personal protective equipment is the last control, and it is not a substitute for a safe method. Mark the work zones on the hazard map and brief the team on where they can and cannot go.

instruction.heading: Dynamic risk assessment and stop-work triggers
instruction.body: A dynamic risk assessment is the process of reassessing risk while work is happening. Set the triggers in advance. Examples include: a new service is found; the ground becomes wet or slippery; a neighbour, child or pet enters the zone; a tool begins to vibrate or cut unevenly; the weather changes; or the material moved is not what was expected. When a trigger occurs, stop the affected work, make the area safe, and review the method. Do not carry on because the job is nearly done. Any worker may stop work when they consider it unsafe, and no worker should be penalised for doing so. Record the trigger, the decision and who was informed. A stop-work decision is a control, not a failure of the crew.

instruction.heading: Site hazard map, verification and escalation
instruction.body: Record the walk-through on a simple two-zone site map. The first zone is the work area, and the second is the buffer area around it where the public or other workers may be. Mark trip hazards, service locations, slopes, pedestrian routes, emergency access and stop-work triggers. Your supervisor should check the decisions you made rather than only the completed map. A competent worker can explain why a method was chosen, what a service means for the work, and which trigger would stop the job. Escalate to the supervisor for any suspected overhead or buried service, any tree that may need a licence to work on, any site that is unsafe to enter, and any hazard you cannot control. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Council permit rules for trees vary; one NSW council's exemption for trees under five metres is an example only. Refer such work and do not begin it.

procedure: Before entering the site, read the job scope and any site notes, and note any known services or hazards.
Walk the perimeter first, then the work area, noting slopes, holes, trip hazards and fragile surfaces.
Identify and mark irrigation components, services and any suspected buried or overhead lines.
Note public and neighbour access, pets, children and vehicle routes into and out of the site.
Choose methods using the hierarchy of control and set safe work zones with barriers or markers.
Set the stop-work and review triggers and brief the team before starting.
Reassess the site at each change of conditions, and stop work when a trigger occurs.
Complete the site hazard map, have the supervisor check it, and keep it with the job record.

workedExamples.situation: A sloping backyard contains a hidden garden hose, uneven pavers and an electrical service box close to the planting bed the client wants cleared.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you mark, what method do you choose, and what needs approval before you start?
workedExamples.reasoning: Mark the hose and the uneven pavers as trip hazards and move the hose out of the path. Mark the service box and keep all cutting tools and cords away from it, using a hand tool in that zone. Set a clear route for barrows that avoids the slope. Do not work on the electrical service box or any cable behind it, because that work is licensed. Refer any question about the service to the supervisor, and record the stop-work trigger for any change in the service's condition.

workedExamples.situation: During clearance, a worker sees a neighbour's child approaching the work area while a powered trimmer is running on the other side of the fence line.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the stop-work trigger, and what happens next?
workedExamples.reasoning: A person entering the work zone is a stop-work trigger. Switch off the trimmer, move it away from the boundary, and ask the adult to take the child back to their property. Restart the work only after the zone is clear and the barrier is in place. Record the event and the decision, and review the zone set-up before the next start.

equipmentAndPpe: Site hazard map template with two-zone layout
Barrier tape, cones and markers for work zones
Measuring tape or marking stakes for slopes and boundaries
Eye protection, gloves and footwear with good grip
First-aid kit and means of communication
Service locating method approved by the business, such as a qualified locating service

commonErrors.error: Walking straight to the job without looking at the perimeter or the buffer area.
commonErrors.prevention: Walk the whole site before equipment is moved, and mark the work zone and buffer on the map.

commonErrors.error: Assuming an unidentified cable or pipe is harmless because it looks old.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat it as live until a qualified person confirms its identity and status. Keep tools away and inform the supervisor.

commonErrors.error: Relying on PPE to cover a hazard that could be removed or separated.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply the hierarchy of control, starting with elimination and separation, before selecting PPE.

commonErrors.error: Continuing work after a trigger because the job is almost complete.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop at the trigger, make the area safe, review the method and record the decision before restarting.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business.

This lesson does not grant a licence to work on electrical services, irrigation mains or any buried or overhead service. Work on those services is outside this business and is not covered by this lesson.
Overhead power lines are a serious electrocution hazard. The 2014 Safe Work Australia guide says no one should enter a no-go zone without the written approval of the electricity supply authority.
The model WHS framework requires duty holders to manage risks to the level that is reasonably practicable, and to rank controls for certain risks, moving from the most reliable option downward.

qualityStandard: A site walk-through is completed and recorded before any equipment is moved.
Every service found or suspected is marked, and no work is done on an unidentified service.
Each work zone and buffer is marked and briefed to the team.
Stop-work triggers are written down before work begins and are reviewed when conditions change.
documentationEvidence: Site hazard map with work zone, buffer zone, services, slopes, pedestrian routes and emergency access.
Stop-work trigger list with the date and the team briefing record.
Record of each trigger that occurred, the decision taken and the person informed.
Photographs of hazards taken with consent and with personal information removed.
summary: The walk-through is the first control. Look at the whole site, including the buffer and the overhead and buried services.
Choose methods by working down the hierarchy of control. PPE comes last.
Set stop-work triggers before work begins, and stop when one occurs.
This lesson does not grant a licence.

knowledgeChecks.question: During a walk-through, a worker finds a meter box and an unlabelled pipe cover at the edge of the lawn. What is the correct action?
options: Assume the pipe is old and cut the grass around it with a powered trimmer, since the pipe is clearly not live today.
Mark the area, keep tools away and inform the supervisor, treating the service as live until a qualified person confirms otherwise.
Cover the pipe cover with soil so that it is not damaged by the mower and the crew can finish the lawn quickly and cleanly.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which order best describes the hierarchy of control when planning a garden method?
options: PPE first, then separation, then elimination, since the crew should start with what they wear and carry.
Administrative controls first, then PPE, then elimination, since procedures are the quickest way to act.
Elimination, substitution, separation and engineering or administrative controls, with PPE last.

knowledgeChecks.question: A tree on the site appears to need work that will take the crew near a power line. What is the correct decision?
options: Stop, record the scope, and refer the work to a licence holder, because work near power lines is excluded from this business.
Proceed with care, since the crew has done similar work before and knows the line clearance rules well enough by now
Ask the neighbour to hold the branch while the crew cuts it, so the branch does not fall on the power line itself

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these does the lesson give as an example of a trigger for reviewing the risk assessment?
options: A neighbour, child or pet enters the zone
